title: Mexico’s Electoral Institute Under Lorenzo Córdova Implicated in USAIDgate
author: Aníbal García Fernández
content:
_This article by[Aníbal García
Fernández](https://contralinea.com.mx/author/anibal/) originally appeared in
the [November 25, 2026 edition of
Contralínea](https://contralinea.com.mx/analisis/ine-de-lorenzo-cordova-
implicado-en-el-usaidgate/), a Mexican investigative journalism magazine._

_The portal of the defunct USAID has published nearly 300 documents containing
internal files, emails and agency analyses that account for millions in
funding for media-related activities. The files include emails with companies
such as Meta, Google, YouTube and WhatsApp, and even millions in funding to
counter Russia and China. In addition, one of the documents reveals indirect
funding to the INE during Lorenzo Córdova’s tenure._

![Screenshot of a declassified USAID / IFES
document](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/cordova-
usaid-02-doc.png)Image: USAID / IFES documents, via Contralínea

Following the closure of USAID by Donald Trump, many non-governmental
organizations, foundations, institutions and media outlets around the world
were left without funding. Now, the portal of the defunct USAID has published
nearly 300 documents containing internal files, emails and agency analyses
that account for millions in funding for media-related activities.

Among the files are emails with transnational corporations such as Meta,
Google, YouTube and WhatsApp, and even millions in funding to counter Russia
and China. In addition, one of the documents reveals indirect funding to the
National Electoral Institute (INE) during Lorenzo Córdova’s tenure.

An example of the close collaboration between USAID and the digital
corporations are the emails exchanged by Ben Supple—a former Meta executive
who, between May 2020 and August 2023, served as global director of
partnerships with the public sector and nonprofit organizations for Meta
Business Messaging (WhatsApp, Messenger and Instagram)—with Zecharia ‘Zack’
Kahn, former acting director of IT operations at USAID and current chief
information officer of the Smithsonian Institution. The latter is an expert in
information technology modernization, cybersecurity and digital strategy.

![Screenshot of a declassified USAID / IFES
document](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/cordova-
usaid-03-doc.png)Image: USAID / IFES documents, via Contralínea

### **Lorenzo Córdova’s INE, IFES and USAID**

In the declassified files, one of the categories is the fight against what
USAID—under the Joe Biden administration—called disinformation. Under that
category, a file from the International Foundation for Electoral Systems
(IFES) dated August 2019 was revealed, titled “Social Media, Disinformation
and Electoral Integrity.”

![Screenshot of a declassified USAID / IFES
document](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/cordova-
usaid-04-doc.png)Image: USAID / IFES documents, via Contralínea

That text contains a section titled: **“Current Responses of Government
Emergency Bodies to Disinformation,” which details the top-down guidance from
IFES to government bodies.** Among the things that **IFES achieved in the
countries where it has a presence, including Mexico,** is **“direct
coordination of government bodies with technology companies; fact-checking;
voter education; identification of disinformation threats and strategic and
crisis planning to address them; and coordination of government bodies with
other state bodies.”**

In that regard, the National Electoral Institute—under the administration of
Lorenzo Córdova, its former president councilor and today a member of the
Somos party—was one of the institutions IFES worked with. On this, the
document states: **“in Mexico, the National Electoral Institute signed a
Memorandum of Understanding and collaborated with Facebook during the 2018
elections, and in Estonia, the State Electoral Office is monitoring online
media in cooperation with other authorities and private companies such as
Facebook and Google**. **The actions available to technology companies include
flagging or removing false content, rating content according to the findings
of fact-checkers, modifying their algorithms to promote truthful information
and hide false information, and ad disclosure policies**. Facebook, for
example, has begun to modify its ad disclosure policies and has experimented
with detecting false content. These changes are not implemented globally, but
are adapted to the context of each country.”

![Screenshot of a declassified USAID / IFES
document](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/cordova-
usaid-05-doc.png)Image: USAID / IFES documents, via Contralínea

It also mentions that **Mexico was a pioneer in this type of program that
USAID promoted and funded through foundations such as IFES**. The same
document states that “**Mexico’s electoral bodies have maintained a focus on
innovation in the area of disinformation. The National Electoral Institute
(INE) is the first electoral body in the world to have memoranda of
understanding with Facebook, Twitter and Google.** The 2014 reforms to the
Mexican electoral process gave the Electoral Tribunal of the Federal Judiciary
(TEPJF) jurisdiction over complaints related to electoral campaigns and the
media. The TEPJF must adopt binding decisions in cases related to the use of
social media, disinformation strategies and other new features of democracy in
the digital age, even where no rules exist. The TEPJF made several notable
decisions in this area during the 2018 electoral process, including protecting
freedom of expression and promoting access to fact-checkers as a response to
fake news.”

![Screenshot of a declassified USAID / IFES
document](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/cordova-
usaid-06-doc.jpg)Image: USAID / IFES documents, via Contralínea

Lorenzo Córdova’s ties to institutions associated with USAID or with the coup-
backing National Endowment for Democracy were sealed during the tour he made
of the United States in 2023, the year his tenure at the INE ended. Before
leaving office, he met with staff from IFES, the NED, the International
Republican Institute (IRI) and the National Democratic Institute (NDI), the
latter two part of the network that makes up the NED. He also visited
conservative think tanks such as the Atlantic Council, NATO’s political arm,
and the Wilson Center.

![Screenshot of a declassified USAID / IFES
document](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/cordova-
usaid-07-doc.png)Image: USAID / IFES documents, via Contralínea

The Mexican electoral institute’s ties to IFES are not new; in fact, since the
former Federal Electoral Institute (IFE) there was already a memorandum of
understanding between the two institutions, so there is a line of continuity
between Córdova’s INE and the IFE of his predecessor and fellow Somos member,
Leonardo Valdés Zurita.

![Screenshot of a declassified USAID / IFES
document](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/cordova-
usaid-08-doc.png)Image: USAID / IFES documents, via Contralínea

![Screenshot of a declassified USAID / IFES
document](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/cordova-
usaid-09-doc.png)Image: USAID / IFES documents, via Contralínea

### **Global Funding**

In the USAID files—published by the US State Department—one can see the
millions that USAID granted to programs of the Center for Democracy, Human
Rights and Governance, such as “Governance, anti-corruption, human rights,
resurgent authoritarianism, rule of law, civil society, media, labor, cross-
sectoral programs, elections and political processes.”

Notable, for example, are 2.4 billion dollars since 2016 for programs focused
on democracy, of which 1.6 billion were administered by USAID and of which 130
million funded the Center for Democracy, Human Rights and Governance.

![Screenshot of a declassified USAID / IFES
document](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/cordova-
usaid-10-doc.png)Image: USAID / IFES documents, via Contralínea

One of the documents released by the Trump administration itself shows funding
by region and program from the State Department’s International Narcotics
Control and Law Enforcement. For fiscal year 2020, this institution granted
funding for programs such as Human Rights (193 million dollars), Governance
(463 million dollars), Civil Society (388 million dollars) and media (158
million dollars).

![Screenshot of a declassified USAID / IFES
document](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/cordova-
usaid-11-doc.png)Image: USAID / IFES documents, via Contralínea

Another of the funded projects was Governance and Anti-Corruption. Under this
heading, the supposed focus was “to build more effective, responsive and
accountable institutions, improve the capacity to mobilize and use resources
to meet public needs, strengthen the ecosystem to fight corruption.”
